extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy, scientific method, and critical thinking (including reviewers assessing arguments and evidence)
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and judge defects in reasoning and observation (a priori errors, non-observation, mal-observation, and faulty generalization) when assessing arguments, claims, or empirical evidence. Emphasis is on diagnosis of the specific logical or evidential error and its practical examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: A priori fallacies
rubrics_metrics.description: Errors that arise from reasoning a priori (from assumed principles rather than empirical evidence), e.g. asserting 'Tout ce qui est vrai de l'effet, est vrai de la cause' or that 'the law of causality holds only between homogeneous things.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid inferring properties of causes from properties of effects on purely a priori grounds. The page gives examples (Victor Cousin, Coleridge, Spinoza, Leibnitz, Malebranche, Descartes) showing how such reasoning leads to false conclusions (e.g. denying mind-matter interaction, positing pre-established harmony, deriving physics from assumed divine perfection). Check whether claims rest on observation/experiment or solely on assumed analogies between cause and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confusing cause and effect / conflating states
rubrics_metrics.description: Treating an effect or a mental state as if it were the cause or conflating distinct kinds of states (e.g. Mill's critique of the Zoonomia: ideas described as 'animal motions of the organs of sense').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating an account distinguish clearly between the phenomenon (effect) and the proposed physical or causal basis. Ask whether the author is describing consciousness or the presumed nervous state, and avoid accepting statements that define the phenomenon as identical with its hypothesized cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-observation — overlooking instances
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-observation occurs when the error consists in overlooking or neglecting facts or particulars which ought to have been observed (e.g., ignoring falsifying instances of a prophet's predictions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether relevant counterexamples were sought or recorded. Look for omitted negative cases and consider whether the evidence set is biased toward confirming instances. Require examination of falsifying observations before accepting an induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-observation — overlooking material circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Failing to observe important circumstances of instances (e.g., not noticing that fulfilled predictions were due to collusion, or overlooking gaseous products in combustion experiments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether all materially relevant conditions and by-products were observed and accounted for. In experimental or historical claims, check for hidden or neglected circumstances that could explain results (collusion, concurrent treatments, unmeasured products).

rubrics_metrics.name: Selective/simple enumeration (per enumerationem simplicem)
rubrics_metrics.description: Generalizing from any instances that occur or are remembered rather than seeking instances decisive of the question — 'generalizing from any which occur, or rather which are remembered.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demand systematic sampling aimed at decisive cases rather than relying on convenient or memorable examples. Beware inductive claims built from anecdotal or selectively collected instances; require criteria for representative or decisive evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to eliminate chance
rubrics_metrics.description: Not reflecting on 'the number of instances requisite for the Elimination of Chance' so that casual coincidences are mistaken for causal relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require consideration of how likely observed correspondences are due to chance. For inductive claims, assess sample size, expected coincidence rates, and whether chance has been plausibly ruled out before inferring causal connection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability / affirmative-instance bias
rubrics_metrics.description: The mind is 'more moved by Affirmativis than Negativis' — striking positive instances are remembered and reported while negative instances are neglected, producing an impression of regularity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging evidence, look for systematically missing negative instances. Give greater weight to negative evidence when testing axioms or general claims. Require that both confirming and disconfirming instances be sought and recorded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preconceived-opinion bias (theory-driven non-observation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A preconceived opinion or theory causes observers to overlook facts contradictory to that opinion; travelers, historians, and devotees read only what confirms prior beliefs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether the observer's prior theory shaped what they attended to or reported. Actively search for observations that would falsify the claimed theory; consider alternative hypotheses rather than allowing a dominant theory to filter perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-observation of unseen or reasoning-dependent factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Overlooking factors knowable only by reasoning (not direct senses) that would change conclusions (e.g., political-economy examples where visible immediate gains mask widely diffused opposite effects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For claims about social, economic, or causal systems, evaluate reasoning that accounts for indirect, dispersed, or delayed consequences. Insist that inferences include analysis of less obvious, distributive effects, not just immediate visible outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution errors from overlooked concurrent causes (medical examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ascribing efficacy to a mysterious or single remedy while overlooking concurrent, causally relevant treatments or conditions (e.g., sympathetic powder applied while wounds were kept closed; cures due to rest and regimen misattributed to plasters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating causal claims about remedies or interventions, examine all simultaneous measures and natural history of the condition. Require controlled separation of candidate causes or clear accounting of concurrent treatments before attributing efficacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mal-observation — mistaking inference for perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Mal-observation is when something seen is seen wrong: mistaking inference for direct perception (e.g., people 'saw' the sun rising and inferred motion rather than appearance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require clear distinction between what was actually perceived and what was inferred. In testimony and description, separate raw sensory report from interpretive claims. Cross-examine witnesses/claims to isolate perception from hypothesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacies of Generalization / improper induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Generalizations that are groundless because they violate the legitimate rules of induction — committed 'on principle' by misconceiving the inductive process rather than by casual lapse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether inductive methods conform to established rules (adequate sampling, elimination of chance, consideration of negative instances, control of confounders). Flag generalizations that rest on a fundamentally erroneous conception of how evidence supports a universal claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confounding observation with rhetorical or emotional persuasion
rubrics_metrics.description: Allowing the love of the marvelous or strong affective response to affirmative instances to substitute for proper evidential weighing (e.g., superstition sustained by attention to fulfilling instances).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of psychological drivers (wonder, envy, moral sentiment) that bias attention and memory. Require disciplined, dispassionate appraisal of evidence rather than reliance on emotionally striking anecdotes.
